content: Tansy, scientifically known as Tanacetum vulgare, is a perennial herbaceous flowering plant belonging to the Asteraceae family. It is native to temperate regions of Europe and Asia but has been introduced to other parts of the world, where it has sometimes become invasive. The plant is also referred to by various common names, including Common Tansy, Bitter Buttons, Cow Bitter, Mugwort, and Golden Buttons. Description Tansy is characterized by its finely divided compound leaves and yellow, button-like flowers. The plant has a robust, somewhat reddish, erect stem that is typically smooth and grows to a height of 50–150 cm, branching near the top. Its leaves are alternately arranged, measuring 10–15 cm in length, and are pinnately lobed. The lobes are deeply divided into smaller segments with serrated edges, giving the leaves a fern-like appearance. The yellow, flat-topped, button-like flower heads are produced in terminal clusters during mid to late summer. The plant emits a scent reminiscent of camphor, with subtle notes of rosemary. Both the leaves and flowers are considered toxic if consumed in large quantities. The volatile oil of tansy contains high levels of thujone, a compound also found in absinthe, which can induce convulsions. Interestingly, certain insects, such as the tansy beetle, have developed resistance to the plant's toxicity and rely on it as their primary food source. History and Distribution Tansy is native to Eurasia and is widely distributed across mainland Europe, though it is absent from Siberia and some Mediterranean islands. The ancient Greeks are believed to have been the first to cultivate tansy for medicinal purposes. By 1525, it was listed in Britain as an essential plant for gardens, under the spelling Tanseye. Culinary Uses Historically, tansy was used as a flavoring agent in puddings and omelets, though its culinary use has largely fallen out of favor. In earlier times, it was highly regarded for its taste, as noted by herbalist John Gerard, who described tansy confections as pleasant in taste and recommended them as a remedy for gout when consumed in moderation on an empty stomach. In Yorkshire, tansy and caraway seeds were traditionally incorporated into biscuits served at funerals. According to liquor historian A.J. Baime, Jack Daniel, the founder of Tennessee whiskey, enjoyed his whiskey mixed with sugar and crushed tansy leaves. Ethnomedical Use Tansy has a long history of use as a medicinal herb. In Irish folklore from the mid-1800s, bathing in a solution of tansy and salt was believed to alleviate joint pain. Bitter tea made from the blossoms of T. vulgare has been used for centuries as an anthelmintic (vermifuge) to expel intestinal worms. Tansy cakes were traditionally consumed during Lent due to the superstition that eating fish during this period caused intestinal worms. It is important to note that only T. vulgare is used in medicinal preparations, as all tansy species are toxic, and overdoses can be fatal. The dried flowering herb of tansy has been used in ethnomedicine to treat migraines, neuralgia, and rheumatism, as well as for its anthelmintic properties. However, its use should be supervised by a qualified herbalist to avoid potential toxicity. Historically, tansy was also employed for its emmenagogue effects, but it has been implicated in cases of miscarriage. Pregnant women are strongly advised to avoid this herb. Other Uses In England, tansy was traditionally used as a natural insect repellent. Bunches of the plant were placed at windows to deter flies, and sprigs were added to bedding and linens to ward off pests. Tansy is also utilized by some traditional dyers to produce a golden-yellow pigment. The dried yellow flowers are often used in floral arrangements. Additionally, tansy serves as a companion plant, particularly for cucurbits like cucumbers and squash, as well as for roses and various berries. It is believed to repel ants, cucumber beetles, Japanese beetles, squash bugs, and certain flying insects. Tansy in Art and Literature Tansy has been celebrated in art and literature. A portion of a 19th-century poem by John Clare describes the beauty of tansy and other herbs in a garden setting, evoking a sense of nostalgia and delight. The poem, titled The Cross Roads; or, The Haymaker's Story, is available through Project Gutenberg.
